sentences: A woman with a long face fills the canvas.
There is no decoration and no setting to speak of, only one person's face, and yet once you meet it, it is hard to look away.
It is a quiet picture, but a powerful one.
The painter is Na Hye-seok, born in Suwon in 1896.
She studied Western painting in Tokyo and is often called Korea's first woman painter in Western oils, a true pioneer.
She was also a writer whose stories and essays spoke frankly about women's lives.
In 1921 she held a solo show of oil paintings in Seoul, remembered as the first exhibition by a Korean woman painter.
In 1927 she set off on a journey around the world that lasted well over a year and a half, taking her across Europe.
During the trip she stayed in Paris and studied at the Académie Ranson.
This portrait is thought to date from that Paris stay, which is why it is usually given as about 1928.
Let's move closer to the face.
Orange shadows fall across her cheekbones.
They carve out the planes of the face sharply, and give the whole head a firm, strong presence.
Instead of plain grey or brown, the shadows themselves carry colour.
Yet her large, deep eyes seem unsettled.
Compared with the firm face around them, they hold something like hesitation or unease.
Her tightly closed mouth, drawn in a straight line, is in shade as well.
It is as if the face says one thing and the eyes another.
Look at the wavy hair, the dark jacket and the pale collar.
This is not hanbok but the look of a 1920s New Woman, and it tells us how the painter wished to present herself.
For a Korean woman of her time, these were bold choices.
The background is split in two, with a blue-black curtain on one side and a brown wall on the other.
These deep, heavy colours push the figure forward and lend the whole picture a calm, solemn weight.
The brushwork is worth a close look too.
Its dark, flat strokes break with the brighter Impressionist manner of her earlier work.
It shows how much one painter's style could change within just a few years.
Some have remarked that the features look almost Western.
Her family, however, always attributed it to her as a self-portrait, and in 2015 her descendants gave it to the Suwon Museum of Art in her hometown.
It is said never to have been shown in an outside exhibition before.
Step back and look again.
Which is the painter's true feeling, the strong face or the restless eyes?
Imagine a woman nearly a century ago, far from home, facing herself in the mirror.
